stories.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.titleZh: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.author: jaz
summaryZh: watch nowNvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO, effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk." President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.Shares of Nvidia closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6."I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia stock chart.Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said. Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations. Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy." He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.""On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote. Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX, Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.Read more Nvidia newsHuang reinstatement reignites voter angst over tech's outsized powerJensen Huang's Nvidia return highlights U.S.-China AI talent raceNvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh's push to read market signals: LiesmanAI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeezeJensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession planTrump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in WashingtonAG Blanche, FBI's Patel dodge questions about Huang investigationCongress blasts Nvidia bringing Jensen Huang backJensen Huang to face Congress the same day as Nvidia GTCFor weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it.""The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China. Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips."The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement Monday. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify.Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls.""Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday.WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huangwatch now

comments.author: icyfox
comments.textZhHtml:
Some takes (and from talking to nvidia people):

- Delaware precedent in Caremark has a very high bar for culpability of boards in matters like this. So I suspect the combination of DoJ saying they won't prosecute combined with this standard will successfully remove their individual liability.

- I'm surprised this decision was completely unanimous at the board level, considering how they quickly forced him out. Full 180 in under two weeks.

- The news media is really confusing selling chips to Megaspeed then hosting them in Malaysia (giving chinese companies access - afaik still legal under the old export regime) and Megaspeed smuggling these physical chips for hosting in Chinese data centers. Former was legal and second was not.

- I would not be surprised if a pardon was mentioned at some point. Will be watching how state AGs end up getting involved. CA has already subpoenaed Nvidia for this.

- There was a drum circle at Nvidia from employees who were petitioning to get him back

Disclosure: I co-host a podcast that talks about this. More discussion if anyone is interested: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t8nLiELIhwA

comments.author: DrScientist
comments.textZhHtml:
Why? I'd contend it is based on a false premise - that secure digital comms is at the heart of crime and terrorism.

If I look at domestic terrorism events in the UK - most appear to have been done by individuals inspired by an idea rather than being part of some secret organisation held together by encrypted comms.

Likewise crime is either out of desperation, haphazard or done by people with severe problems.

Organised crime on the other hand requires both trust and fear, the sort that uses in person meetings to build and maintain.

I'd turn the 'if you have nothing to hide, why worry' argument on it's head.

If you have a reason to worry, why use digital encrption comms - when you can just meet in person or use very simple pre-agreed code phrases etc?

I accept that you can use mass surveillance to pick up suspicious behaviour of those lone terrorists ( internet history, purchase history etc ) - however such a tool in the wrong hands is much more dangerous than a few individuals in my view.

Bottom line if the law is such that the authorities can see everything as a matter of course, then organised crimimals won't be using it in a way that can be surveilled...

stories.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
stories.author: janvdberg
summaryZh: Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux. I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^) Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional. This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that. If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol. Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

A huge lots of congratulations to the Ladybird team. What a wonderful accomplishment truly this is.

comments.author: simscitizen
comments.textZhHtml:
Browsers are runtimes and webpages are apps. They just happen to be apps that are dynamically fetched over the network and are packaged as HTML/CSS/JS instead of as PE/ELF/Mach-O binaries.

Runtimes can have bugs or inefficiencies that cause them to use more memory than strictly necessary, but by and large most memory problems are the product of the apps (or webpages) themselves.

comments.author: panta
comments.textZhHtml: The view of web pages as apps and browsers as runtime environments/OSes is reasonable but in my opinion it even reinforces the idea that it should be the browser duty to contain bad behavior from web apps/pages. Browsers are well positioned to do so, as they know exactly which resources are used by each tab , and how those grow over time. Also browsers already treat web content as untrusted (sandboxing, isolation), so it would be a natural next step to extend that approach to resource usage. It would match how Operating Systems work, where it's the OS acting as an "arbiter", not the userland application.

stories.title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
stories.titleZh: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
stories.author: zdw
summaryZh: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by Automotive News. The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses.Discussions are starting with Japan’s domestic suppliers, though international suppliers will be looped in soon.Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images|Getty ImagesThe first discussions of standardization are set to include Japan’s domestic automotive parts suppliers, though international suppliers will be brought into the fold in time. The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report.The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into new innovations.“We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato said. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.”➡️ Skip the lot. I love the transparency, or at least given technical details, that Zhipu provide - a refreshing change from the locked-down approach of the western companies, and an interesting glimpse into the direction of SOTA LLMs.

Looped Transformers are an obvious direction even if there are still problems to be worked out. The original Transformer is a bit like an unrolled for loop, and rather unnaturally pairs different sets of weights, both for attention and feed forward (knowledge) with different "layers" (aka loop iterations). Far more natural is to strive for something more like our brain's thalamo-cortical loop and association cortex, where "thought" is iterative and there are no restrictions as to what patterns/knowledge get applied when.

A similar idea has been explored before ("Universal Transformer", 2019), seemingly going nowhere, but perhaps "necessity is the mother of invention" and compute-starved Chinese companies are finding a way to make it work.

comments.author: noddybear
comments.textZhHtml: A normal transformer has N layers, all of which are run forward for each token. A looped transformer is a bit different. Instead of N layers, it has K. These K layers are then looped, such that the output (not a token) of the first run of these K are fed back into the start of the K layer block. This looping happens until a fixed-point is achieved (i.e another loop results in a noop). At that point, a token is sampled. This means that tokens get different amounts of compute, depending on how challenging they are.

summaryZh: In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?

Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing. So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working. It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask. So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone??? This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet! Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra. Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget. And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now. This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for me and have my best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example. On the existential threat or tool question, I'm firmly in the tool camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions.

comments.author: Lerc
comments.textZhHtml:
A LLM should be considered an advisor to the same extent as legal, financial, and medical. They should be legally required to act to the best of their capability in the interests of their client, subject to the same requirements that they don't break the law to do so as applies to legal, financial, or medical advisors.

An important part of that is that they must never represent themselves as acting for someone who is not their client.

This still allows them to work for you while being the client of their parent companies, but it would disallow claiming to be serving a client when that person is not their client.

When an AI says it is serving your best interests, it must actually be doing so.

The nature of client confidentiality is that it exists because in order to advise appropriately, a full understanding of the client's situation might be necessary. The legal protection of confidentiality enables disclosing the required information without fear of making it public. That too should be protected with AI in your service.

All of this is established principle. I don't see any reason why this should not be applied to AI as well. The same principles have the same reasoning as the current legally protected advisors.

This is an absolute must for the common benefit to society. The alternative is a world where people increasingly trust the ever-more-reasonable sounding AIs while the answer to the question "Who should I vote for?" is available to the highest bidder.

Agree. I wonder how long it took for these advisory professions to be held to that standard. I can't speak for the rest of the world, but it seems to be something we're still grappling with today in the UK and the regulation of these professions has been decades if not centuries in the making.

Confidentially is an interesting aspect of it because it doesn't apply to all of those professions equally and at there are quite a few limitations to it - for example in the UK:

- A solicitor/barrister has to keep things confidential, but also has to act honestly based on what they know - so if they know you're guilty because of what you've told them, their advocacy for you has to be focused on testing the evidence against you and trying to cast reasonable doubt rather than pushing a narrative they know to be false (or they can recuse themselves so you can start again with new representation).

- Doctors are expected to maintain confidentiality, but may have a duty or discretion to disclose when other people are at risk and your confidentiality is also weighed against your capability to manage your own health affairs.

- Accountants and tax advisers keep your financials confidential, but have to disclose tax evasion and money laundering.

All of those things require those advisors to have actual independence in their judgements and actions and relies on them being subject to disciplinary action. That feels quite different from what we have with frontier AI models today. The models would need to have some memory that spans every interaction in order to properly understand whether they were acting within your best interests and to continuously weigh their duty to you against their duty to everyone else.
